doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Return to New York in the late 1960s
title: Archie Shepp calls him to Newport in 1968
summary: Shepp and Leroy Williams find Ware in the street, he plays Newport on borrowed bass, and Shepp keeps hiring him.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Then Sonny Rollins had a -- let me see. No, Archie Shappeldon (PHONETIC) -- now, I'd never -- I only worked one job with Archie. I knew him before I went back to Chicago. I played a little loft thing with him, he and Bill Dixon. That was back before I got sick. Had to be the early '60s. I didn't pay too much attention to what they were talking about avant the garde. I just played whatever came into my head, whether it was inside or outside. They took it on out, you know what I mean, which was beautiful. I ran into Archie when he come through Chicago with Coltrane. They played out there at Soldiers Field, and anyway, I run up on him one night -- he run up on me. It was in '68, Newport was going on.
About 2:00 in the morning, he and the drummer, a

friend of mine from Chicago, Leroy Williams, had settled in New York, and he was looking for me. I'm walking down the street -- I had just left Billy Greene's brother's house, little Donald Greene, and I'm on my way home. It was about 2:00 in the morning. This car pulls right up on the sidewalk and blocked my path. So I'm wondering what's going on. Two guys jumped out and it's Leroy and Archie Shepp. Archie say, "Man, you going up to Newport. Play tomorrow afternoon." I say, "Wait a minute, man. I can't play your music," you know. He said, "Well, you been playing my music all --" he didn't call me Wilbur. He used to call me Mr. Ware and I used to get kind of P-offed at him because I thought he was putting me on. He said, "No, Mr. Ware, you're an elder statesman," and he always talked like that.

But I said, "Okay, I'll go." He didn't really have to twist my arm too much. I wanted to see what Newport was like. I hadn't been up there since the riot. Anyway, we took off that night. We got to Newport the next afternoon and they had us sandwiched in. He had Howard Johnson on tuba. He had Grachan Moncur on trombone, himself on tenor, and he had a poet, crazy guy, Leon Bibbs (PHONETIC) -- not Leon Bibbs, but --
Leroy Bibbs. He's nuts. He was in the same vein, you might say, Lenny Bruce and all the cats like that, which you would call -- I won't say beat poet, a hippie

Anyway, they had sandwiched us in between -- they was waiting on Clark Terry's big band to show up and Elvin and Jimmy Garrison and Joe Farrell was playing before we was scheduled to come on and, oh, they did it. Elvin sounded so beautiful. Standing ovation and we had to follow them. I didn't even take a bass up there because I figured I could borrow somebody's bass. I was asking Joe Benjamin (PHONETIC) -- Joe Benjamin was going to play next with Clark Terry, so I asked him can I use his bass. He said, 'No, you should have brought yours.' Jimmy Garrison said, 'Man, here, take my fiddle,' which was beautiful. Jimmy was like that. And we played and George Weim Williams (PHONETIC) only let us play one tune, but we played that and played it well. Had a conga player Muhammed Ali, who happened to be Rashid Ali's brother.

From that moment on, every job that Archie Shepp would get, he'd call me. 'Mr. Ware --' record dates, jobs, we played up in Buffalo. They had some whole week of music, quite a few groups -- Cannonball, Mongo, Tito Puente (PHONETIC). Philly Billy Joe Jones worked with us, Archie Shep (PHONETIC), Tommy Turrentine and little blind Chris Anderson and Joe Lee Wilson. That's the group that Archie Shepp took up.
